note: Equity and Trusts. Deliberately statute-anchored: where a proposition here has no statutory source it is stated as doctrine, without a case citation, pending a verification pass. See docs/STYLE.md, 'Never invent a citation'.

cards.front: Which provision brings English equity into Malaysian law?
cards.back: Section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956 — the rules of equity as administered in England at a fixed date, so far as local circumstances permit and subject to local written law.

cards.front: Does English equity decided after the reception date automatically apply in Malaysia?
cards.back: No. Section 3 fixes reception at a date. A later English decision may persuade a Malaysian court, but adopting it is that court's choice.

cards.front: What are the two limits written into the reception of equity?
cards.back: It applies only so far as local circumstances permit, and it yields to local written law.

cards.front: Equity acts *in personam*. What does that mean in practice?
cards.back: It works on the conscience of a named person and orders them to act. It does not by itself alter a register or bind the world.

cards.front: Where a rule of equity and a rule of common law conflict, which prevails?
cards.back: Equity. That is the point of having a second system — it exists to correct hard answers the first one gives.
cards.source: Standard statement of the relationship between the two systems.

cards.front: A claimant seeking an equitable remedy behaved badly in the same matter. What should you reach for?
cards.back: Clean hands. Equity may refuse a claimant whose own conduct in the transaction was improper, however strong the claim looks.

cards.front: A claimant sat on an equitable right for many years. What should you reach for?
cards.back: Delay. Equity may treat a long-unasserted right as abandoned, and this is an argument about the claimant's conduct rather than the merits.

cards.front: What does a trust split in two?
cards.back: Ownership. The trustee holds the legal title; the beneficiary is entitled to the benefit. The trustee's duties are owed to, and enforceable by, the beneficiary.

cards.front: Name the three roles in an express trust.
cards.back: The settlor creates it, the trustee holds the property, the beneficiary takes the benefit. One person can occupy more than one role.

cards.front: What three things must be certain before a court will find an express trust?
cards.back: Intention, subject matter, and objects. All three, and each failure has its own consequence.

cards.front: What does certainty of intention actually test?
cards.back: Whether a duty was imposed on the holder. If they could honestly keep the property and breach nothing, there is no trust — whatever words were used.

cards.front: A settlement covers "some of my shares". Which certainty is in trouble, and why?
cards.back: Subject matter. A court cannot administer property it cannot identify, so no trust arises over an unidentified part of a holding.

cards.front: Why is certainty of objects necessary?
cards.back: A trustee's duties are owed to the beneficiaries. Without an identifiable beneficiary there is nobody with standing to enforce them and nothing for a court to supervise.
A trust that sends the benefit back to the person who provided the property, where no gift was intended. It arises by operation of law, not by arrangement.
A trust imposed by law on a person whose conscience is affected — for instance someone who takes property knowing it was meant for another. Nobody agrees to it.
